chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
title: Passing as Cubans in Miami
summary: Billed as imported from Cuba, the mixed band avoided Florida segregation and Machito posed as interpreter for American-born Leslie Johnakins.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Okay - ahh - in 1945, the Machito orchestra was in Florida and I understand there was racial problems down there because the Machito orchestra was down there at a club. Do you recall this time period I am talking about?

Definetely. You see, the fellow that took us to Miami - ahh - he was very smart fellow, so he publicized that we was imported from Cuba. We was in love with New York--Machito and his Afro-Cubans, from Cuba, so as a native from Cuba, we got away with -- my band was black and white......
but they wouldn't discriminate against you because you were Cubans.

... so, we even have a body-guard to take care of us and they transport us to Miami Beach. From Miami Beach to the city and then I used to live in a white hotel. I never had problem, we used to eat in Miami City, in those

white restaurants, as a matter of fact, I used to be a cashier because we finished at our club about four o'clock in the morning, so the owner of the place, the restaurant, I think it is 8th St. or somehow, from across the church. There was a restaurant, a beautiful restaurant, that practically everyone went up there. Could you believe that I was the interpreter of Johnakins, because I want Johnakins to speak English with that heavy accent for a black, I mean ...
You are talking about Leslie Johnakins.
Right. I don't want him to ask for a -- I was the -Johnakins' interpreter, like he doesn't know English.
I see. So you wanted to ..... to avoid ....
... keep the secret from them, that you were really black men from New York City; so being from Cuba now made the difference.
